subject: Banking
title: Jérôme Kerviel's €50 Billion Bet
description: A 60-second lesson on Jérôme Kerviel's €50 Billion Bet.

hook.text: Jérôme Kerviel at Société Générale built a hidden €50 billion position — more than the bank's entire market value.

buildup.text: Kerviel was a junior trader in Paris. He bypassed controls using his knowledge of back office systems from a prior role.

discovery.text: The losses reached €4.9 billion when the bank discovered and unwound his positions.

twist.text: Kerviel claimed his managers knew about his positions.

climax.text: Banks celebrated Kerviel's profits and ignored his methods.

punchline.text: €50 billion in hidden bets. Profitable? Hero. Unprofitable? Rogue trader.

quiz.question: How large was Kerviel's hidden position compared to Société Générale?
options: Larger than the bank's entire market value

details.summary: French trader Jerome Kerviel secretly built a $50 billion position at Societe Generale through fake hedging trades, causing a $7.2 billion loss when unwound in 2008, the largest rogue trading loss at the time.
details.whyItMatters: Kerviel's case exposed how a single junior trader could bypass risk controls at a major bank. It revealed that banks' internal safeguards were far weaker than they publicly claimed.
takeaways: Kerviel built unauthorized positions worth $50 billion
His fake hedges fooled the bank's risk management systems
Societe Generale lost $7.2 billion unwinding his trades in a crash

faq.question: How did Kerviel hide $50 billion in trades?
faq.answer: He used his knowledge of the bank's back-office systems from a previous compliance role. He created fictitious offsetting trades that made his positions appear hedged, fooling automated risk checks.

faq.question: Was Kerviel solely responsible for the losses?
faq.answer: Kerviel argued the bank knew about his positions and profited when they were winning. A French court initially convicted him but later ruled Societe Generale shared responsibility for inadequate controls.
